clue.text: We're all in the same old boat !

definitions.text: We're all in the same old boat !

parts.words: We're all in the same old boat
parts.note: the nation's islanders all share one country, and Brunel's famous old steamship carried the same name

explanation.surface: A rueful remark that everyone shares the same predicament.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'in the same boat' means sharing a plight; here the boat is literal: Brunel's iron steamship SS Great Britain, launched in 1843, and 'we' are all its inhabitants.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is home to all of 'us', and the historic ship of 1843 bears the same name.

clue.text: Polished work of Derbyshire

definitions.note: the definition names a place of that county, a town in the High Peak

parts.note: something polished has a gloss, a shiny finish
OP is short for opus, Latin for a work

explanation.surface: A fine piece of craftsmanship from Derbyshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'polished work' as fine craftsmanship; the definition is 'of Derbyshire', a town in that English county in the Peak District.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town in the High Peak district of the English county, near Manchester.

clue.text: From 'the north the next person to gain artistic distinction, what's more

annotationWithheld.why: From the north the next person to gain artistic distinction, what's more (5): 'what's more' defines EXTRA and 'artistic distinction' is RA, but no reading of 'From the north the next person' gives EXT or reverses to it.
annotationWithheld.clue: From 'the north the next person to gain artistic distinction, what's more

clue.text: We've no coin to buy one at this price

definitions.text: We've no coin to buy one at this price

parts.words: We've no coin to buy one at this price
parts.note: at a price of two for a penny, a single item would cost a halfpenny's half, a coin never minted

explanation.surface: A shopper laments having no money to buy one at the price asked.
explanation.walkthrough: At two items for a penny one costs a halfpenny, and you cannot buy just one without splitting the pair; the phrase also means cheap and common.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means cheap and plentiful, things sold at two for a single penny.

clue.text: Phoned with news of a step up in the world ?

annotationWithheld.why: Phoned with news of a step up in the world ? (4): the clue gives RUNG (phoned; a step of a ladder) but the held answer is RING, and the grid's checked letters cannot separate them.
annotationWithheld.clue: Phoned with news of a step up in the world ?

clue.text: Heads or tails, the matador's unlucky

explanation.surface: A bullfighter's fate decided by the flip of a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin is flipped to call heads or tails, and an unlucky bullfighter is thrown into the air by the bull's horns.

clue.text: No end of dailies coming up with an epic story

indicators.note: in a down entry the remaining letters are read upwards, from bottom to top
the word's ending, its last two letters, is cut away

explanation.surface: Newspapers serialising a grand epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' removes ES from DAILIES, leaving DAILI; 'coming up' turns it backwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's epic poem tells of the siege of Troy and the wrath of Achilles.

clue.text: Man with a jaw like a Dutch uncle's

definitions.text: Man with a jaw like a Dutch uncle's

parts.words: Man with a jaw like a Dutch uncle's
parts.note: a jaw is a long talk or reprimand, and a Dutch uncle is someone who lectures sternly

explanation.surface: A description of a man's heavy jawline resembling a Dutchman's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jaw' looks like the face; it is slang for a long talk, and to talk like a Dutch uncle is to admonish someone frankly.
explanation.definitionFit: A university teacher who gives long talks, a jaw being slang for a long-winded address.

clue.text: Treat a fellow to a beer

parts.note: Reg is a man's name, a typical fellow
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Buying a man a pint.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain someone lavishly, especially with food and drink.

clue.text: Excursion expenses

explanation.surface: Money spent on a day trip.
explanation.definitionFit: An outing or trip out is an old sense of the word; in the plural it is also money paid out, expenditure.

clue.text: But not a peaceful influence in the Saga

definitions.text: But not a peaceful influence in the Saga

parts.words: But not a peaceful influence in the Saga
parts.note: the heroine's name comes from the Greek goddess of peace, yet in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga she causes discord

explanation.surface: A remark that someone in a family saga stirred up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But not' plays on the name meaning 'peace' in Greek; the Saga is Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga, where Soames Forsyte's wife is the source of family strife.
explanation.definitionFit: The Forsyte Saga's disruptive wife bears a name taken from the Greek goddess of peace.

clue.text: Like England in need of Milton, Wordsworth said — or in need of drainage ?

definitions.text: Like England in need of Milton, Wordsworth said — or in need of drainage

parts.words: Like England in need of Milton, Wordsworth said — or in need of drainage
parts.note: Wordsworth's sonnet 'London, 1802' calls England, needing Milton, a fen of stagnant waters, and land needing drainage is boggy

explanation.surface: A literary note on Wordsworth's view of England's need for Milton.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's sonnet begins 'Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour: England hath need of thee: she is a fen of stagnant waters' - so England is fen-like, boggy land that wants draining.
explanation.definitionFit: A fen of stagnant water is marshy, boggy ground, the kind of land that needs draining.

clue.text: Feudal pursuit

parts.note: read not as a medieval lord's pastime but as the pursuit of a feud, a long-running quarrel

explanation.surface: A medieval pastime such as hawking or jousting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feudal' suggests the Middle Ages and the feudal system; here it means 'of a feud', and the pursuit is a long blood feud.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running blood feud between families is the classic quarrel carried on over generations.

clue.text: She presided over the dessert

parts.note: the Roman goddess of fruit and orchards rules over the fruit course served at the end of a meal

explanation.surface: A hostess sitting at the head of the table for the pudding course.
explanation.walkthrough: Dessert in older usage was the fruit course; the Roman goddess of fruit trees and orchards presides over it. 'The dessert' looks like a misspelt 'desert'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of fruit and orchards watches over fruit, the traditional dessert course.

clue.text: How a rill came to provide power

definitions.text: How a rill came to provide power

indicators.note: asks in what manner the words are put together, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An account of how a small stream was put to work driving machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' asks for the letters of RILL CAME to be rearranged; the whole clue also describes a channel bringing water to turn a mill wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A channel carrying a fast current of water to drive a mill wheel.

clue.text: He sharply reduces our cash in hand

definitions.text: He sharply reduces our cash in hand

parts.words: He sharply reduces our cash in hand
parts.note: a pickpocket of old cut the strings of a purse with a sharp knife, so our ready money is cut away

explanation.surface: A complaint about someone, such as a tax official, cutting our available funds.
explanation.walkthrough: Purses once hung from belts on strings; the thief sliced them with a knife, so 'sharply reduces' is literal. 'Cash in hand' sounds like accounting.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a pickpocket, who sliced through the strings holding a purse.

clue.text: Bedstraw for the friendly Bottom, say ?

indicators.note: signals that the words are pronounced, giving a word that sounds like them

parts.note: friendly means pally, and Bottom is the weaver turned into an ass in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: Straw bedding laid out for a sociable Shakespearean character.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is the weaver given an ass's head in A Midsummer Night's Dream; 'say' signals that PALLY ASS is spoken aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A mattress stuffed with straw, a bed of straw.

clue.text: A lovely shrub for loam, Gina

indicators.note: the shrub's letters are given in exchange for those of the following words, rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice that a beautiful bush suits loamy soil, addressed to Gina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' signals swapping the letters of LOAM and GINA for a new arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A flowering tree or shrub prized for its large showy blooms.

clue.text: "My stars !" said the cow jumping over the moon

definitions.text: "My stars !" said the cow jumping over the moon

parts.words: "My stars !" said the cow jumping over the moon
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme cow, leaping over the moon, could claim the galaxy as her own, its name suggesting milk

explanation.surface: The cow of the nursery rhyme exclaims in surprise as she leaps over the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My stars!' is an old exclamation of surprise; read literally, the cow claims as her own the galaxy whose name suggests milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Our galaxy is named for its pale band across the night sky, likened to spilt milk.

clue.text: Least exclusive millinery

parts.note: headwear for the crowd, the common people, rather than for the select few

explanation.surface: A remark about the most downmarket hat shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The mob is the least exclusive group of all, the common crowd; the cap here is a frilled cotton bonnet worn indoors by women in the 18th century.
explanation.definitionFit: A frilled cotton bonnet worn indoors by women in the 18th and 19th centuries.

clue.text: By Clara I am called a Goth

indicators.note: the letters of the words before are what 'I am called' when rearranged into a name

explanation.surface: Someone named Clara labels me a barbarian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Am called' signals that CLARA I is shuffled into a name: the Visigoth king who sacked Rome in 410.
explanation.definitionFit: He was king of the Visigoths, the Germanic people who sacked Rome in AD 410.

clue.text: Work-hook it!

explanation.surface: A curt order to someone to get out.
explanation.definitionFit: It is needlework done with a single hooked needle, and as a verb it means to make something with that tool.

clue.text: It signifies a switch in penal procedure

definitions.text: It signifies a switch in penal procedure

parts.words: It signifies a switch in penal procedure
parts.note: a switch here is a thin cane of twigs used for flogging, not a change of policy

explanation.surface: A remark about a change in the way offenders are punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A switch' looks like a change of policy; it is a flexible rod, and the birch was a bundle of twigs once used to flog offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Flogging offenders with a bundle of twigs was a judicial punishment in Britain until 1948.

clue.text: Overheated, the Spanish guest house

parts.note: something overheated is hot
el is the Spanish word for 'the'

explanation.surface: Complaint about a stuffy Spanish boarding house.
explanation.definitionFit: A place offering lodging to paying travellers.

clue.text: What's that — fell flat in one of Sofia's cobbled streets ?

definitions.note: the definition is a description, 'what fell flat', of a thing that failed: a noun phrase

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of words that follows, across the join between them

explanation.surface: Someone takes a tumble on the cobbles of a street in Sofia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals letters lodged inside 'Sofia's cobbled' (soFIA'S CObbled). The definition 'What's that — fell flat' is a riddle: a thing that fell flat, a total flop.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete and humiliating failure, something that fell flat, from the Italian for a flask.

clue.text: With tender signs I depart to Eire

parts.note: the symbols on British money of old: s for shillings and the L-shaped pound sign, from Latin librae
to depart is to go

explanation.surface: A traveller leaves for Ireland with some money in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was counted in pounds, shillings and pence, written with £ (an L) and s; that legal tender gives SL. The definition names a county and town in the Irish Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: A town and county in the north-west of the Irish Republic.

clue.text: Recruit's raw

indicators.note: read as 'has', the word holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: A new soldier is inexperienced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raw' looks like a recruit's inexperience; it is the colour of unbleached linen, French for raw.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for raw or unbleached, naming the pale fawn colour of undyed linen.

clue.text: Some hat, mon!

parts.note: a Highlander's cry of admiration at showy headgear, and the Berkshire race meeting famous for elaborate millinery

explanation.surface: A Scotsman admires a striking hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mon' is Scots dialect for 'man', so the speaker is a Scotsman; the answer split in two says just that, and Royal Ascot, the Berkshire race meeting, is famous for flamboyant hats.
explanation.definitionFit: The Berkshire racecourse's royal meeting is famous for showy hats, and also names a broad cravat.

clue.text: O's butt

parts.note: O is love, the zero score in tennis, and a butt is the target of laughter

explanation.surface: The bottom end of the letter O.
explanation.walkthrough: O is 'love' (nil in tennis), and a butt is someone laughed at; the proverb 'Love laughs at locksmiths' says love gets past any lock.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says love laughs at the maker of locks, so he is love's laughing stock.

clue.text: The one with youth on the prow

definitions.text: The one with youth on the prow

parts.words: The one with youth on the prow
parts.note: Gray's poem The Bard pictures a gilded vessel with Youth on the prow and Pleasure at the helm

explanation.surface: A description of a vessel with a young person standing at its bow.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's The Bard has 'Youth on the prow, and Pleasure at the helm'; the boat in the line is steered by Pleasure, hence a vessel for enjoyment.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel used for recreation, recalling Gray's line where Pleasure steers and Youth stands at the bow.
